text: I am trying to remember now where it was, and when it was, that it hit me.

I am trying to remember now where it was, and when it was, that it hit
me.

text: Was it during my first walk along the Bund in Shanghai in 2005?
text_raw: Was it during my first walk along the Bund in Shanghai in 2005?

text: Was it amid the smog and dust of Chongqing, listening to a local Communist Party official describe a vast mound of rubble as the future financial centre of South-west China?
text_raw:
Was it amid the smog and dust of Chongqing, listening to a local
Communist Party official describe a vast mound of rubble as the future
financial centre of South-west China?

text: That was in 2008, and somehow it impressed me more than all the synchronized razzamatazz of the Olympic opening ceremony in Beijing.

That was in 2008, and somehow it
impressed me more than all the synchronized razzamatazz of the
Olympic opening ceremony in Beijing.

text: Or was it at Carnegie Hall in 2009, as I sat mesmerized by the music of Angel Lam, the dazzlingly gifted young Chinese composer who personifies the Orientalization of classical music?

2009, as I sat mesmerized by the music of Angel Lam, the dazzlingly

classical music?

text: I think maybe it was only then that I really got the point about the first decade of the twenty-first century, just as it was drawing to a close: that we are living through the end of 500 years of Western ascendancy.
text_raw:
I think maybe it was only then that I really got the point
about the first decade of the twenty-first century, just as it was drawing to
a close: that we are living through the end of 500 years of Western
ascendancy.

text: The principal question addressed by this book increasingly seems to me the most interesting question a historian of the modern era can ask.
text_raw:
The principal question addressed by this book increasingly seems to
me the most interesting question a historian of the modern era can ask.

text: Just why, beginning around 1500, did a few small polities on the western end of the Eurasian landmass come to dominate the rest of the world, including the more populous and in many ways more sophisticated societies of Eastern Eurasia?
text_raw:
Just why, beginning around 1500, did a few small polities on the western
end of the Eurasian landmass come to dominate the rest of the world,
including the more populous and in many ways more sophisticated
societies of Eastern Eurasia?

text: My subsidiary question is this: if we can come up with a good explanation for the West’s past ascendancy, can we then offer a prognosis for its future?
text_raw:
My subsidiary question is this: if we can
come up with a good explanation for the West’s past ascendancy, can we
then offer a prognosis for its future?

text: Is this really the end of the West’s world and the advent of a new Eastern epoch?
text_raw:
Is this really the end of the West’s
world and the advent of a new Eastern epoch?

text: Put differently, are we witnessing the waning of an age when the greater part of humanity was more or less subordinated to the civilization that arose in Western Europe in the wake of the Renaissance and Reformation – the civilization that, propelled by the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment, spread across the Atlantic and as far as the Antipodes, finally reaching its apogee during the Ages of Revolution, Industry and Empire?

in the past, not least in their probable duration, but also in our greater
degree of physical comfort, we must exercise our imaginations quite
vigorously to understand the men and women of the past.

text: In his Theory of Moral Sentiments , written a century and half before Collingwood’s memoir, the great economist and social theorist Adam Smith defined why a civilized society is not a war of all against all – because it is based on sympathy:
text_raw:
In his 
Theory of
Moral Sentiments
, written a century and half before Collingwood’s
memoir, the great economist and social theorist Adam Smith defined why
a civilized society is not a war of all against all – because it is based on
sympathy:

text: As we have no immediate experience of what other men feel, we can form no idea of the manner in which they are affected, but by conceiving what we ourselves should feel in the like situation.
text_raw:
As we have no immediate experience of what other men feel, we can form no idea
of the manner in which they are affected, but by conceiving what we ourselves
should feel in the like situation.

text: Though our brother is on the rack, as long as we ourselves are at our ease, our senses will never inform us of what he suffers.
text_raw:
Though our brother is on the rack, as long as we
ourselves are at our ease, our senses will never inform us of what he suffers.

text: They never did, and never can, carry us beyond our own person, and it is by the imagination only that we can form any conception of what are his sensations.
text_raw:
They
never did, and never can, carry us beyond our own person, and it is by the
imagination only that we can form any conception of what are his sensations.

text: Neither can that faculty help us to this any other way, than by representing to us what would be our own, if we were in his case.
text_raw:
Neither can that faculty help us to this any other way, than by representing to us
what would be our own, if we were in his case.

text: It is the impressions of our own senses only, not those of his, which our imaginations copy.

It is the impressions of our own
senses only, not those of his, which our imaginations copy.

text: By the imagination, we place ourselves in his situation.
text_raw:
By the imagination, we
place ourselves in his situation.

text: In 1909, inspired by a visit to Japan, the French-Jewish banker and philanthropist Albert Kahn * set out to create an album of colour photographs of people from every corner of the world.

philanthropist Albert Kahn
*

photographs of people from every corner of the world.

text: The aim, Kahn said, was ‘To put into effect a sort of photographic inventory of the surface of the globe as inhabited and developed by Man at the beginning of the twentieth century.’ Created with the newly invented autochrome process, the 72,000 photographs and 100 hours of film in Kahn’s ‘archives of the planet’ show a dazzling variety of costumes and fashions from more than fifty different countries: dirt-poor peasants in the Gaeltacht, dishevelled conscripts in Bulgaria, forbidding chieftains in Arabia, stark-naked warriors in Dahomey, garlanded maharajas in India, come-hither priestesses in Indo-China and strangely stolid-looking cowboys in the Wild West.
